episode_title: The Brave New Future of Electricity

stories.topic: What's Water? The Plug Point as the Unseen
stories.summary: Amit explains that the name of his podcast, The Seen and the Unseen, began with Bastiat's idea of the unintended consequences of public policy. Over time it came to mean the hidden layers behind society and our own minds, including the things we stop noticing. He recalls David Foster Wallace's story of one fish asking another 'how's the water today?' and the second replying 'what's water?' For us, electricity is that water: we plug in and it simply works. He invites the listener to dive into the plug point and travel down the wire to see what lies at the other end.
stories.insight: The systems that matter most are often the ones we have stopped seeing. Curiosity starts by treating the ordinary as strange.
stories.quote: And one aspect of what is unseen to me is the things that we normalize in our lives. That are almost like the oxygen in the air that we breathe.

stories.summary: Ajay imagines taking a time machine to Akbar, the most powerful ruler of the Middle Ages, and telling him that you can plug something in, flick a switch, and magic happens. Electricity is technology so advanced it is indistinguishable from magic. Yet we have become 'dumb users' who flick switches and get a bill at month's end (or, in parts of India, steal the power).
stories.insight: By historical standards, an ordinary person today commands powers no emperor ever had, and we barely notice.
stories.quote: You went to Akbar and you told him, I can plug in this and flick a switch and all kinds of magic happens. It's magic, okay?

stories.summary: Solar panel costs have fallen at a compound rate of roughly 20–25% a year for 30 years. Ajay recalls that Shockley, one of the three Bell Labs scientists who invented the transistor, derived from quantum mechanics a ceiling on how much sunlight a silicon cell can turn into electricity. Ajay remembers the figure as about twelve percent. Engineers didn't accept defeat. They tried other materials and stacked layers, so that light passing through one layer is captured by the next.
stories.insight: A physical limit binds a particular design, not the goal. Ingenuity gets past it by changing the approach.
stories.quote: you can never stop human ingenuity. So the human started thinking very well, I won't use silicon. I'll start using other materials. I will start sandwiching them in multiple layers.

stories.summary: A windmill sounds simple, but its progress has been a chain of ambitions. First, go higher, because winds are stronger aloft, as any kite flier knows. Then build giant blades that are light and strong and last 25 years. Then go offshore, where the flat sea gives stronger winds and allows even bigger machines: roughly 100-metre blades on each side, mounted on steel pylons driven into India's shallow coastal shelf, with the power carried back to land.
stories.insight: Big engineering leaps are usually a sequence of solved sub-problems, each one unlocking the next.
stories.quote: Then they got unhappy, you know, I'm trapped by the surly bonds of earth. I want to go even higher. I want bigger, better, more. So they thought let's go offshore.

stories.summary: Ajay remembers when the big puzzle was making tungsten bulbs last longer by filling them with a noble gas so the filament wouldn't oxidize. Tube lights then improved efficiency. But a tungsten bulb puts out 10% of its energy as light and 90% as heat, so it is really a heater. LEDs reached about 90% efficiency. White LED light required cracking blue LEDs, which Japanese scientists at UC Santa Barbara achieved. The exotic technology was then mass-produced and is now everywhere in India.
stories.insight: The energy revolution is not only about new power sources. Demand-side efficiency is a miracle in its own right.
stories.quote: So roughly speaking in a tungsten bulb, ten percent of the energy goes out as light, ninety percent goes out as heat. It's actually a heater.

stories.summary: On many summer days in Germany, the price of electricity falls to zero because there is so much solar capacity, and Germany isn't even very sunny. India has perhaps 250–275 days of bright sun. If it got the economics right, afternoon power could be free there too. Ajay's favourite consequence is charging your EV, and a backup battery pack, for free every afternoon, so that personal transport costs only the price of the vehicle.
stories.insight: Renewables create stretches of near-free energy. The big opportunity is to reorganise life and business around them.
stories.quote: Germany actually doesn't get a whole lot of sunlight. Imagine in India if you could get this right, the sunlight is plentiful.

stories.summary: Growing up, Ajay heard vague claims that Middle Eastern states cut off oil to India during the 1971 Bangladesh war. The story supposedly didn't matter only because the war lasted 14 days and the Pakistani army surrendered. It nagged at him: had Saudi Arabia been colluding with the US? He felt something that big couldn't be left as a vague allegation. So he reached a personal friend of a former Indian ambassador to Saudi Arabia, and learned it never happened. It was a made-up rumour meant to paint those states as hostile to India.
stories.insight: Don't let convenient national myths settle in your head as facts. Trace them to a source, and especially those that feed a 'toxic brew' in foreign policy.
stories.quote: And I have it on full authority that no, this never happened. It's just a vague rumor that was made up to try to portray the Middle Eastern states as being hostile to India.

stories.topic: Kalpakkam Seen from the Finance Ministry
stories.summary: While at the Ministry of Finance, before the Indo-US nuclear deal, Ajay realised that private firms in the US and France were building commercially competitive reactors. India's reactors were science projects. Once the Kalpakkam facility's costs were reckoned correctly, it simply wasn't competitive. Private outfits like Westinghouse are cost-conscious and risk-taking. Meanwhile, the era when Homi Bhabha, India's best and brightest, worked for the state (at an institution funded first by the Tatas, then by the government) is gone. The modern Indian state no longer attracts that level of talent.
stories.insight: Proving you can build something and building it competitively are different games. Pride in the first shouldn't block buying the second.
stories.quote: Reactors were being made in India as a science project, as a demonstrator that you know some Sarkari scientists know how to make a reactor, which is nice.

stories.topic: Manmohan Singh Stakes His Job on the Nuclear Deal
stories.summary: Amit praises Manmohan Singh for pushing through the Indo-US nuclear deal with George W. Bush despite opposition from the Left parties and Sonia Gandhi's reluctance. Singh said he would not stay prime minister if he couldn't do it. Ajay adds the backdrop: India's military and foreign-policy establishment leaned towards the USSR. The rapprochement with the US came from the imagination of leaders like Narasimha Rao, Vajpayee, Jaswant Singh and Manmohan Singh, not from the bureaucracy. The sour coda is that India's nuclear liability rules mean not one American or French reactor has arrived since.
stories.insight: Leaders can break institutional inertia, but a downstream rule can quietly cancel a historic win.
stories.quote: Manmohan took a firm stand and said that I will not be prime minister if I cannot do this because it's good for the country.

stories.summary: India spends military and diplomatic effort protecting Bhutan from Chinese incursions, as Doklam in 2017 showed. In return, Indian companies build and run hydel plants in Bhutan, send the power back to India, and pay Bhutan rent for the sites. Indian engineering, Indian utilities, Indian demand and a Bhutanese site add up to a pragmatic deal. Nepal has vast hydel potential that fits perfectly: glaciers melt in summer just when North India runs its ACs. But the relationship is broken by toxic fights over its constitution and the idea of a Hindu state, so the deals never happen.
stories.insight: Unemotional 'who has the skill, who has the site, who has the demand' deals beat nationalism. The gap between Bhutan and Nepal shows what bad foreign policy costs.
stories.quote: This is an unemotional sensible business arrangement.

stories.summary: Ajay likens offshore wind off Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka to the UK's North Sea oil and gas: a bounty only a government with policy muscle can reap. Electricity is a state subject, so Tamil Nadu must first fix its own system. Evening peak prices, not flat-priced 25-year power purchase agreements, are what make offshore wind pay, so builders should be risk-takers who can go bankrupt. Then India must mend ties with Sri Lanka so Indian firms can build on Sri Lankan sites and bring the power ashore in Tamil Nadu. That would make Tamil Nadu a renewable-energy paradise for exporters facing carbon taxes. Amit pegs the needed investment at around 14 lakh crore rupees.
stories.insight: Natural endowments are only potential. Institutions and diplomacy decide whether a region cashes them in.
stories.quote: It is theirs to win, it is theirs to lose.

stories.topic: Why Amit Takes an Uber Despite Owning a Car
stories.summary: Looking for other uses of the price system, Amit messaged his Takshashila friends, and Nitin Pai suggested car parking. On one side of a wall, real estate (especially Mumbai rent) is exorbitant. On the other side, the road, parking is free. So whoever gets there first takes the spot, need doesn't matter, and there are parking shortages everywhere. That is why Amit, who owns a small car he likes, often takes an Uber or public transport in Bombay.
stories.insight: A zero price on a scarce resource doesn't make it free. It makes it unavailable, and everyone pays in other ways.
stories.quote: But on the other side it is free. It doesn't make sense. It means that whoever can get in there gets in there.

recommendations.item: World Energy Outlook 2023
recommendations.creator: International Energy Agency
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation of the week: the IEA's October 2023 energy report.
recommendations.reason: He admits people flee from reports as boring official platitudes, but calls this one unputdownable. Energy is 'pure drama' right now, and the report's facts, graphs and stories make that vivid. Never read a report, he says, but make an exception for this one.

recommendations.item: Midnight in Chernobyl
recommendations.creator: Adam Higginbotham
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation of the week, tied to the nuclear chapter.
recommendations.reason: Gripping non-fiction reportage on what happened behind the scenes at Chernobyl. Amit finds the TV series pretty good, but prefers the book. It shows the disaster as a failure of the Soviet state, rooted in the system's structure and incentives so that it seems bound to happen. It also reminds Indian readers that their own state was then a 'fax copy' of the Soviet model. Above all, it's a crackling read.

recommendations.item: Nuclear Power Can Save the World
recommendations.creator: Joshua S Goldstein, Staffan A Qvist & Steven Pinker
recommendations.context: The New York Times essay Amit reads from while making the case for nuclear power.
recommendations.reason: It puts nuclear safety in perspective. Sixty years of nuclear deaths, Chernobyl included, roughly equal one month of coal-related deaths. And 60 years of American nuclear waste could fit in a single Walmart.

recommendations.item: That Which is Seen, and That Which is Not Seen
recommendations.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
recommendations.context: Mentioned at the start as the essay that inspired the name of Amit's podcast The Seen and the Unseen.
recommendations.reason: The original statement of the unintended consequences of public policy, the idea behind Amit's whole way of looking at the world. He promises to discuss it in the next episode.

recommendations.item: This is Water
recommendations.creator: David Foster Wallace
recommendations.context: Source of the two-fish story that opens the episode.
recommendations.reason: Its parable, where a fish asks 'what's water?', captures how the things we normalise become invisible. That is the lens Amit uses to examine electricity.

recommendations.item: Anupam Manur's piece on the Bangalore water crisis
recommendations.creator: Anupam Manur
recommendations.context: Brought up while discussing other uses of the price system, amid Bangalore's water shortage.
recommendations.reason: Amit urges everyone to read it because it is so counterintuitive. Pricing water helps the poor, since the current system effectively redistributes from the poor to the rich who use far more water.

recommendations.item: Making Policy Fun with Khyati Pathak and Friends (Episode 374, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Khyati Pathak, Anupam Manur and Pranay Kotasthane
recommendations.context: Released the same week; Amit cites it as where the Bangalore water-pricing discussion came up.
recommendations.reason: A conversation with Takshashila friends that includes Anupam Manur's case for pricing water, the same logic this episode applies to electricity.

recommendations.item: The Great Redistribution
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's own earlier column, cited while generalising the water-pricing argument.
recommendations.reason: It argues, using tariffs as the main example, that interference with free markets amounts to redistributing wealth from the poor to the rich.

recommendations.item: Pranay Kotasthane's post on plasma and organ sales
recommendations.creator: Pranay Kotasthane
recommendations.context: Linked when Amit lists organ sales as a domain where markets could work.
recommendations.reason: Pranay lays out the economic logic for allowing sales and how it works in other parts of the world. Amit thinks the topic deserves a whole episode.

recommendations.item: Sell the Tiger to Save It
recommendations.creator: Barun Mitra
recommendations.context: Recalled as an old example of counterintuitive price-system thinking, written for the New York Times.
recommendations.reason: It argues that legalising the sale of tigers would make people breed them, as they breed cows or chickens, and so save the species. That runs against the reflex to ban everything.

recommendations.item: Solving the intermittency of renewables
recommendations.creator: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Show-notes companion to Ajay's chapters on the evening-peak problem and storage.
recommendations.reason: Deeper reading on the episode's central puzzle: how to cope when solar disappears exactly as evening demand surges.

recommendations.item: Offshore wind in Tamil Nadu: from potential to reality
recommendations.creator: Akshay Jaitly, Charmi Mehta, Renuka Sane & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Show-notes companion to Ajay's argument about the offshore wind bounty off Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka.
recommendations.reason: The detailed case behind Ajay's claim that Tamil Nadu must build the policy capability to unlock offshore wind.

recommendations.item: A new dawn for nuclear energy?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Show-notes companion to the nuclear chapter.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's own writing on nuclear energy, which goes with his argument for separating nuclear weapons from nuclear power and treating reactors as a business.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Show-notes link to an earlier long-form conversation on the same subject.
recommendations.reason: A longer treatment of the climate-change and power-sector themes this episode compresses.

recommendations.reason: The fuller argument on why agriculture is held back by the absence of the price system.

recommendations.item: Fixing Indian Education (Episode 185, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: Amit names education as another domain where state control causes suffering.
recommendations.reason: A deep dive into what's broken in Indian education and how to fix it.

recommendations.item: Education in India (Episode 77, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Amit Chandra
recommendations.context: Linked alongside the other education episode.
recommendations.reason: An earlier conversation on Indian education, another field the episode says suffers from keeping prices out.

recommendations.item: We Love Vaccines! We Love Freedom! (Episode 27, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Show-notes link accompanying Ajay's point about vaccine pricing.
recommendations.reason: Goes with Ajay's argument that COVID vaccine makers were paid far less than the trillions of dollars of value they created. Letting prices rise would allocate vaccines better and fund research for the next pandemic.

recommendations.item: Son of Bosey
recommendations.creator: Anand Ramachandran
recommendations.context: Mentioned while Amit explains the Chennai slang 'blade'.
recommendations.reason: The great blog of Anand Ramachandran, whom Amit calls perhaps the funniest man in Indian history.

core_ideas.explanation: One person switching a TV on or off is random, but thousands of households cancel each other out. That makes demand smooth and forecastable, just as an insurer can predict daily car crashes even though each crash surprises the driver. Grid managers forecast demand in 15-minute slots using weather, cricket matches and other variables, then choose the cheapest way to meet it.
core_ideas.quote: While the electricity decisions of any individual putting on and off one switch are random. By the time you get down to any kind of geographical aggregation, then cancelling out happens and there's an insurance like character and it becomes highly predictable.

core_ideas.concept: The Old World: Planners, Slow Coal and Canteen Contractors
core_ideas.explanation: In the old system, government grid managers work like air traffic controllers, frantically matching supply to demand slot by slot. Coal plants take hours to spin up or down, so sudden swings must be met by fast gas and hydel. Private generators are not real businesses. They sit on 25-year contracts with fixed returns, take no risk and do no thinking. The government does all the business thinking, and the waste shows up as expensive electricity.
core_ideas.quote: It is not a world of business. It is really you're just a canteen contractor to the government.

core_ideas.explanation: Twenty-five years ago, net zero looked impossible because civilisation runs on fossil fuels, and many thought the planet was headed to become Venus. Then came a run of miracles: solar costs falling 20–25% a year for 30 years, giant offshore wind, and LEDs jumping lighting efficiency from 10% to 90%. Geothermal and geologic hydrogen are now on the horizon.
core_ideas.quote: So you know, one should never count out human innovation. One should never count out the power of the human mind.

core_ideas.concept: The Cruel Mismatch: Sun at Noon, Demand at Dusk
core_ideas.explanation: Solar floods the grid in the afternoon, but demand spikes in the evening. People come home and switch on lights, ACs and TVs, and fridge compressors kick in, all at once. Gas and hydel can't cover the gap, and coal can't run flat-out all day. The old grid has no good answer, and the renewable revolution has made the planners' lives harder.
core_ideas.quote: So at the worst possible time, your best possible source goes away. Like what could be more cruel than this?

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues the bottleneck is no longer science but human institutions that 'did not get the memo' that the world has changed. Amit's image for this is the 'tube light' state, the Indian slang for someone slow on the uptake. Reality changes, and the state struggles to catch up 10–20 years later.
core_ideas.quote: So what has happened is a miracle. And then old institutions are the bottleneck.

core_ideas.concept: A Gap Between Supply and Demand Calls for Prices
core_ideas.explanation: Whenever you hear 'reconcile supply and demand', the answer is the price system, which goes back to Adam Smith in 1776. Grid engineers can only order suppliers around because consumers face a fixed price. The efficient route is for both sides to adjust. Let prices fall to near zero on sunny afternoons and rise to 15, 25 or 50 rupees a unit in the evening, and nobody should cry profiteering.
core_ideas.quote: When an economist hears the word shortage, you think price.

core_ideas.explanation: First, demand: people check spot prices on their phones, AC remotes adjust temperature to price, ice is made in the free afternoon, and firms run a daytime shift plus a late-night one while skipping the expensive evening. Second, wind: it keeps blowing after sunset, so it earns the evening premium and attracts investment. Third, storage: batteries, and water pumped from the Konkan up to the Sahyadris by day and released as hydel power at night. Storage operators are simply businesses that buy cheap and sell dear, with no central planner needed.
core_ideas.quote: So the wind guy will get a bad price of electricity through the day when the sun is shining. And make like a bandit in the evening when the price surge comes.

core_ideas.concept: Let Markets, Not Engineers, Pick the Technology Mix
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay rejects the engineer-led, centrally planned vision of the 'right' energy mix. Investors should bet on wind, storage or offshore projects themselves and go bankrupt if they guess wrong. Failure has to be possible, which a 25-year fixed contract never allows.
core_ideas.quote: Our insights into economics guide us that engineering decisions, picking winners or which is the correct technology is something that should be done by market forces and people should take business risk.

core_ideas.explanation: Without prices you get shortages, and the poor already live with them. Under flexible prices, average costs fall thanks to near-free solar afternoons. A poor household could charge an electric two-wheeler at noon, while the rich pay extra to top up their cars in the evening. Amit adds that supply-side innovation lowers prices over time. Ajay's analogy is airfares: red-eye and midday flights are cheap, 8 a.m. flights are dear, and people self-select instead of facing one flat government price.
core_ideas.quote: There is a quaint euphemism in this field, it's called intermittency, which is at random you'll get power cuts.

core_ideas.concept: Nuclear Is the Safest Energy, and Tribalism Hides It
core_ideas.explanation: Coal smoke alone kills more than half a million people a year. In 60 years of nuclear power, only three accidents raised alarm: Three Mile Island killed no one, Fukushima's deaths came from the tsunami and a panicked evacuation, and Chernobyl was the result of Soviet bungling. Twenty-four countries run nuclear power without going on to build bombs. France gets about 71% of its electricity from nuclear, and its grid's carbon per kilowatt-hour is a tenth of the rest of the world's. Amit argues that the 'no nukes' movement of the 70s became green dogma because people think in tribes rather than judging each idea on its merits.
core_ideas.quote: If you care about the environment, if you care about climate change, you should embrace nuclear.

core_ideas.concept: Decouple Nuclear Weapons from Nuclear Energy
core_ideas.explanation: India's nuclear journey, from Homi Bhabha to Indira Gandhi and Pokhran, was a nationalist, self-reliant weapons project, and Ajay sees that story as done. Nuclear energy is a different game. It should belong to private, competitive, global capitalism, which means buying the best and cheapest reactors from whoever makes them.
core_ideas.quote: But you should never conflate nationalistic objectives with the game of achieving economic development.

core_ideas.concept: The Liability Trap and the Promise of SMRs
core_ideas.explanation: India's liability rules hold foreign reactor makers liable forever for any accident, whoever was at fault, so no vendor will sell. This has negated the essence of the Indo-US nuclear deal. The same wall awaits small modular reactors: 50-megawatt 'black boxes' that could sit in a factory corner. They could let, say, an aluminium plant make zero-carbon metal and export to Europe without facing carbon border taxes.
core_ideas.quote: It's like saying I sold you a car and thirty years from now you had an accident and I'm responsible.

core_ideas.concept: Foreign Policy Is About Interests, and Energy Runs Through It
core_ideas.explanation: Amit notes that markets gain from larger networks, and nationalism shrinks them. Ajay argues foreign policy should be deal-making for citizens' welfare, not propaganda or scoring debating points at the UN. Energy shows the stakes: Bhutan's hydel deal is a success, Nepal's untapped hydel is a failure, and the Sri Lanka offshore-wind bounty is waiting. India has failed to give its neighbours a stake in its prosperity, as a European Union-style approach would.
core_ideas.quote: The purpose of foreign policy is to make deals with governments of other countries in the way that best suits the interests of the people of India. It is about interests.

core_ideas.explanation: The logic that fixes electricity applies elsewhere. Price water, which helps the poor. Price parking, since free roadside parking next to exorbitant real estate makes no sense. Privatise garbage collection. Allow organ sales. Legalise selling tigers so people breed them. Pay vaccine makers in line with the trillions of dollars they add to world GDP. Allow a market for surrogacy. Amit adds that every interference with the price system effectively redistributes from the poor to the rich.
core_ideas.quote: the answer everywhere is prices because prices are so powerful in the way that they carry information and incentives.

core_ideas.concept: Conservative and Liberal at Once: the Universal Outlaw
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay calls himself conservative because he opposes social engineering by the state, and liberal because he treats the world as a blank slate to rethink from first principles. That offends both traditionalists and progressives who want the state as a big stick. Amit describes himself as having 'liberal ends but conservative means', in the tradition of Gokhale, Ranade and Agarkar.
core_ideas.quote: I'm a conservative in the sense that I never want social engineering. I never want somebody else to tell us what to do. I'm a liberal in that the world is a blank slate and we should rethink ourselves.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: After Ajay describes asking a coal plant to spin up, Amit deadpans: 'I went to a coal power plant and I said, Hey dude, I need you to spin up and you're right, it was very slow in responding. I didn't hang around for a couple of hours to see if it started responding.'
Ajay on consumers who think power just appears: 'we the fat, indolent, lazy ingrates of the world get this illusion that we just throw a switch and magically the electricity just happens.'

Amit points out that Ajay unknowingly used two slang words, 'blade' (windmill blades) and 'tube light'. 'Blade' is Chennai slang for damn boring, learned from Anand Ramachandran, 'the funniest man in Indian history'. Ajay is the opposite of blade, making engineering so fun Amit would have wanted to be one: 'Thank God I wasn't.' And when it comes to Amit's bad jokes, Ajay is a tube light: 'You get them the next day.'
Ajay on markets: 'every trivial 300 parameter LLM knows that when you say reconcile a gap between supply and demand, that's what the price system does.'
Ajay daydreaming of free afternoon power in India: 'imagine there are no policy mistakes. It's easy if you try.'
Ajay on solar's evening disappearance: 'the sun is a fickle friend. He like misbehaves on you when you need him the most.'

Ajay rehabilitates the hoarder for the battery age: 'hoarders and speculators, the hero of Bengali movies, will come into this business... I can buy at 50 paisa and I can sell at 50 rupees. Great. I'm a banya. I'll make money.'

Amit, after Ajay mocks government canteen contractors: 'some of my closest friends are government canteen contractors. You know, they make great medu vadas. They will be very offended at seeing this episode.'

Amit borrows Ajay's 'Hey, Mr. Gas' for TV news: 'every time I watch news television and I see some random expert spouting yarn on something, I feel like saying to him, Hey, Mr. Gas. Shut the fuck up.'
Ajay after declaring himself both conservative and liberal: 'I've just managed to offend everybody... I'm the universal outlaw. I'm the universal outcast.'

After Ajay describes small modular reactors as black boxes in a factory corner, Amit says: 'I've been in your dinky little Mumbai flat, and one third of the flat is taken up by this big black box. Is it a reactor?'

Ajay casts the offshore wind opportunity as divine exasperation: the good Lord putting a bounty off the coast and saying 'India, Sri Lanka, get your shit together. I'm giving you such a big prize, if only you will understand how to work together.'

Ajay's report recommendation: 'So never ever read a report, but this time make an exception.' Amit: 'I'll make an exception just for you.' Then Amit on Midnight in Chernobyl: 'You can't put it down. Though you should at some point put it down because how long can you carry a book around?'

The episode's arc, from a plug point all the way to foreign policy with Sri Lanka, is Amit's live illustration of the show's title: 'Like who would have thought that you're going to get into a plug point... and end up with foreign policy.'
Ajay channels the line 'sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic', imagining showing a light switch to Akbar.
Shockley, Brattain and Bardeen, the three Bell Labs scientists who invented the transistor, cited by Ajay for Shockley's limit on silicon solar cells.
Adam Smith: 'the amazing solution, the remarkable solution, was in the pages of Adam Smith in 1776', namely let prices move.
Three Mile Island (1979), Fukushima (2011) and Chernobyl (1986), the only three nuclear accidents in 60 years that raised public alarm, per the NYT essay Amit reads.
Homi Bhabha to Indira Gandhi and Pokhran: Ajay's shorthand for India's nationalist nuclear-weapons journey, which 'climaxed in 1974' and which he says is now complete.
G.K. Gokhale, Ranade and Agarkar, the freedom-struggle liberals Amit claims as heroes of 'liberal ends but conservative means'.
Doklam, 2017, cited by Ajay as evidence of the real cost India bears to protect Bhutan.
The UK's North Sea oil and gas, Ajay's analogy for the offshore wind off Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka: a bounty only a policy-capable government can exploit.
Amit on the Indian state of the Chernobyl era: 'in many ways was a fax copy of what the Soviet state was'.
